nodes.title: Tool Tip Ref image auto mode
widgets_values:
This determines what content Ref 0 represents. You need to specify in the prompt how Ref 0 should be used—for example, as the start frame (which is what I use) or for another purpose.

OFF

Only the first clip uses Ref 0 as the start frame.
Ref 0 is not used for any subsequent clips.

Last Frame

Only the first clip uses Ref 0 as the start frame.
Each following clip uses the last frame from the previous clip as its first frame.
The last frame is automatically saved to the output folder for use in the next clip.

Original

Every clip uses Ref 0 as its start frame.
Alternatively, you can define in the prompt how Ref 0 should be used.

nodes.title: TOOL TIP - Promts per CLip
widgets_values:
using [1] ... [2] splits the promt per clip

[1] Opening → controlled camera movement

A cinematic podcast introduction featuring the same attractive adult woman. She is funny, charismatic, naturally expressive, with a warm smile and neat, small eyebrows. She speaks directly to the camera with natural eye contact.

The camera makes one slow, smooth movement toward the subject and gradually arrives at a comfortable presenter distance. The movement stops at this distance. Once the final distance is reached, the camera remains completely stationary.

Keep the entire head, hair, shoulders, and upper body comfortably visible. Plenty of space remains around her head. Never crop or cut off any part of her face or head.

[2] Hold the established distance

Continue directly from the previous shot and preserve the exact established camera distance. Do not move closer. Do not zoom in. Do not push in.

The woman continues speaking naturally to the camera in a comfortable medium presenter framing. Her entire head and shoulders remain visible with clear space around them. Natural hand gestures and facial expressions. The camera stays at the same distance for the entire shot.

[3] Slight camera adjustment, then STOP

Continue from the previous shot at the same comfortable distance. The camera may make a very subtle adjustment in position, but it must not move closer to the woman's face.

Maintain a natural presenter framing with the complete head, hair, shoulders, and some upper body visible. No zoom toward the face. No tightening of the frame. No face-filling crop. After the subtle adjustment, the camera remains completely still.

[4] Side movement only

Continue from the previous shot at the same camera distance. The camera moves gently sideways around the subject into a subtle three-quarter angle, approximately 20–30 degrees.

This is lateral movement, not forward movement. Do not move closer to her. Do not zoom in. Maintain the same comfortable framing and distance. Keep her entire head and shoulders visible with generous space around her face. After reaching the three-quarter angle, the camera stops and remains still.

[5] Final framing — NO MORE ZOOM

Continue from the previous shot with the same camera distance and framing. Do not move closer. Do not zoom in. Do not push toward the face.

The woman finishes her introduction naturally. Maintain a comfortable presenter framing with her entire head, hair, neck, and shoulders visible, plus clear space around her head. The camera remains at this distance for the entire shot. No further camera movement toward the subject. No face crop. No cut-off forehead, hair, chin, or sides of the face.

When finished, manualy clean up the H3 output and Video folders.

nodes.title: FL2VL model promt 1 reference image only
widgets_values:
Subject Definitions

<Subject 1> = the adult woman shown on the left in <Picture 2>.
<Subject 2> = the adult man shown on the right in <Picture 2>.

Use both Subject 1 and Subject 2 throughout the entire video. The final video must contain only these two subjects from the reference images. Do not replace either subject with any person appearing in <Video 1>.

Preserve both subjects' identities with high consistency: recognizable facial features, face shape, hairstyle, skin appearance, body proportions, and overall physical appearance. <Picture 3> shows both subjects in full body and is the primary reference for their clothing, footwear, accessories, and complete outfit. Keep their outfits consistent with <Picture 3> throughout the video.

All Motion and camara positions are Transfered from <Video 1> strictly to both subject. subject 1 and 2 dance the motion/choreography of <Video 1>

Use <Video 1> strictly as a motion/choreography reference-

Extract the movement information from the main character of the <Video 1>, including:

body movements and choreography
gestures and arm/hand movements
leg and foot movements
poses and pose transitions
body orientation and direction changes
timing and rhythm
speed, acceleration, and physical dynamics
dance steps and choreography sequence

Apply the extracted choreography naturally to both Subject 1 and Subject 2. The two subjects must perform the choreography together as the same two people defined by <Picture 2> and <Picture 3>.

If <Video 1> contains multiple dancers or multiple people, do not interpret those people as additional characters in the final video. Treat only the main center dancers in <Video 1> only as motion references. Select the relevant dance motion and adapt it to the two reference subjects.

### Two-Subject Requirement

The final result must contain both the adult woman and the adult man.

 Subject 1 = woman
 Subject 2 = man
 Both must remain present and recognizable.
 Do not merge them into one person.
 Do not omit either subject.
 Do not substitute either subject with a dancer from <Video 1>.
 Do not create a third performer based on <Video 1>.
 Do not transfer the reference dancers' identity or appearance to either subject.

The choreography should be adapted for two performers when necessary. If the reference video shows only one dancer, use that dancer's movement as the choreography source and reproduce the movement simultaneously or naturally adapted for both Subject 1 and Subject 2.

The woman should generally occupy the left side and the man the right side, unless the choreography or camera movement naturally requires them to cross or change positions. Their identities must remain stable even when they change positions.

### Camera

Use <Video 1> as a reference for camera motion only, including camera movement, framing, shot scale, perspective, timing, and composition where appropriate.

The camera must film Subject 1 and Subject 2, not the people from <Video 1>.

### Priority Rules

When there is any conflict between the references, follow this priority:

1. Subject identity and appearance: <Picture 2>
2. Clothing, footwear, and accessories: <Picture 3>
3. Choreography and body motion: <Video 1>
4. Camera movement and composition: <Video 1>

The final output should look like a cinematic music video featuring the exact adult woman and adult man from <Picture 2>/<Picture 3> performing the choreography from <Video 1>.

Critical instruction: <Video 1> provides MOTION ONLY. <Picture 2> and <Picture 3> provide PEOPLE AND APPEARANCE ONLY. Never use the identity or appearance of anyone in <Video 1>.

The final video should look as if <Subject 1> and <Subject 2> are the actual performers filmed using the exact shot language, camera movement, choreography, timing, and visual rhythm of <Video 1>.

When <Video 1> contains one primary dancer, adapt that dancer's choreography naturally so that <Subject 1> and <Subject 2> perform together as two distinct people.

When <Video 1> contains multiple dancers, use the relevant main/central choreography and movement as the reference. Do not interpret the reference dancers as additional characters.

<Subject 1> should generally occupy the left side and <Subject 2> the right side when consistent with the reference choreography. If the choreography naturally requires crossing, turning, repositioning, or changing sides, allow those movements while maintaining each subject's identity.

Maintain strict identity continuity during:

camera movement

rotations

changes of perspective
changes of lighting
rapid movement
pose transitions

The final result contains exactly two human performers: <Subject 1> and <Subject 2>.

<Picture 2> provides the PEOPLE AND IDENTITY.
<Picture 3> provides the CLOTHING, FULL-BODY APPEARANCE, AND ACCESSORIES.
<Video 1> provides the SHOTS, CAMERA, CHOREOGRAPHY, AND MOTION.
